questions.q: What exact verified value does `test_grover_iteration_count_matches_known_value()` lock into the test suite?
options: grover_iteration_count(1024) == 25, matching the (pi/4)*sqrt(1024) ≈ 25.13 value verified in Lesson 19
grover_iteration_count(1024) == 1024
grover_iteration_count(1024) == 32
grover_iteration_count(1024) == 100
questions.explain: The test encodes the exact verified Lesson 19 value -- (pi/4)*sqrt(1024) rounds to 25 -- directly into the test suite, so a future refactor of grover_iteration_count can't silently drift from that confirmed number.

questions.q: What does `test_qaoa_shot_budget_matches_lesson_19_example()` verify, and why does it matter that it matches a specific pre-verified number rather than just checking the function runs without error?
options: It just checks the function doesn't crash, with no specific number involved
It checks qaoa_shot_budget(3, 100, 2000) == 2,400,000, the exact value verified in Lesson 19, pinning the implementation to a number that was independently checked, not just assumed correct
It checks that QAOA always uses exactly 3 layers
It checks the function returns a string, not an integer
questions.explain: Matching the test against the exact 2,400,000 figure independently verified in Lesson 19 means the implementation is checked against ground truth, not just checked for 'runs without crashing' -- catching a formula bug that a crash-free run wouldn't reveal.

questions.q: In `run_qaoa_layer(circuit, backend, shots)`, how is the backend-abstraction requirement from Lesson 21 satisfied?
options: The function hardcodes AerSimulator internally
The function takes backend as a parameter rather than importing or instantiating a concrete backend class itself, matching Lesson 11's injected-backend pattern
The function ignores the backend parameter entirely
The function only works with real hardware, never simulators
questions.explain: run_qaoa_layer receives backend as a parameter and calls backend.run(...), never importing a specific backend class -- directly satisfying the Lesson 21 requirement that backend selection happen via injection, not a hardcoded import.

questions.q: What confidence level does `test_ghz_measurement_distribution` use (via its z-score threshold of 2.58), and why does the lesson emphasize that this threshold is documented rather than left implicit?
options: 95% confidence; documented because it's always the industry default

99% confidence; documented explicitly because, per Lesson 5 and Lesson 7, an undocumented threshold leaves the test's pass/fail verdict unjustified and the same data could pass or fail depending on which threshold was silently assumed
100% confidence, which is only possible with infinite shots
There is no confidence level associated with a z-score threshold
questions.explain: |z| < 2.58 corresponds to roughly 99% confidence (Lesson 7). The lesson emphasizes this must be an explicit, documented choice, since (as Lesson 7's worked examples showed) identical data can pass at one confidence level and fail at another.

questions.q: What is a 'regression-locked value' as the lesson uses the term, and how does `grover_iteration_count`'s test exemplify it?
options: A value that can never be changed under any circumstances
A specific, independently verified numeric result encoded directly into a test so that future code changes can't silently drift away from it without the test failing
A value stored only in a comment, never in executable test code
A randomly generated value used to seed a simulator
questions.explain: A regression-locked value is a verified result (like 25 iterations for N=1024) written into an executable assertion, so any future change to the implementation that would silently alter that known-correct value gets caught by a failing test.
